summary: Presents a mechanism for an ALTO server to push incremental updates to clients using Server-Sent Events, so clients need not re-fetch full network information resources. ALTO provides network-related information that helps applications make better decisions. It is standards-track.

plainLanguage.summary: ALTO servers publish maps that tell applications which network path is cheapest. RFC 8895 lets the server push changes to those maps as they happen, over a connection the client keeps open. The server can send just the part that changed, so the client does not have to download the whole map again.

subtitle: How an ALTO server pushes just the changes in its network information to clients over Server-Sent Events.

tldr.problem: The ALTO protocol is pull-only, so a client can learn about changes to a large network or cost map only by periodically re-fetching the whole thing.
tldr.mechanism: An update stream service keeps an HTTP connection open and sends Server-Sent Events, each carrying either a full replacement or an incremental change, a JSON merge patch or a JSON patch, for one resource. A separate stream control service lets the client add or remove resources.
tldr.outcome: Updates stay small, because only changes are sent, and they arrive immediately, because the server pushes them as soon as they are available.

today: RFC 8895 is a Proposed Standard, published in November 2020. No RFC obsoletes it and no RFC updates it, so it is still the published way for an ALTO server to push updates to its clients.

sections.title: Pushing ALTO Updates to Clients
sections.content:
The Application-Layer Traffic Optimization (ALTO) protocol (RFC 7285) provides network-related information, called network information resources, to client applications so that clients can make informed decisions when using network resources. An ALTO server provides network and cost maps. A network map partitions the set of endpoints into a manageable number of sets, each defined by a Provider-Defined Identifier (PID), and a cost map gives directed costs between those PIDs. Given both maps, an ALTO client can obtain the cost between two endpoints by looking up each endpoint's PID in the network map and then looking up the cost between the two PIDs in the cost map. Such costs let the client choose communicating endpoints with low network costs.

The ALTO protocol defines only a pull model. There is no mechanism for a client to obtain updates to network information resources other than by periodically re-fetching them. In settings where a resource may be large but only parts of it change frequently, for example some entries of a cost map, complete re-fetching can be inefficient.

This document presents a mechanism for an ALTO server to push incremental updates to ALTO clients. Combining server push with incremental updates gives two benefits. Updates can be small, because when only a small section of a resource changes the server can send just the changes. Updates can also be immediate, because the server can send them as soon as they are available. The mechanism is primarily intended for GET-mode network and cost maps, but it can also carry updates for POST-mode ALTO services such as the endpoint property and endpoint cost services, and it can support new ALTO services defined by future extensions.
sections.plainLanguage: ALTO servers publish maps that tell applications which network path is cheapest. RFC 8895 lets the server push changes to those maps as they happen, over a connection the client keeps open. The server can send just the part that changed, so the client does not have to download the whole map again.

sections.title: Two Ways to Encode a Change
sections.content:
The design needs two techniques: a way to encode an incremental change, and a way for the server to push it. For encoding, the RFC uses JSON merge patch and JSON patch, and it gives a non-normative summary of each.

JSON merge patch (RFC 7396) defines an encoding for incremental changes used by the HTTP PATCH method. This document adopts only the merge patch object encoding and does not use the PATCH method, because the updates are sent as events rather than HTTP methods and they travel from server to client. Informally, a merge patch transforms one JSON value into another using a recursive algorithm. The two values are treated as trees of nested JSON objects, the leaves are values such as arrays, strings and numbers, and the path to each leaf is the sequence of keys leading to it. When the updated tree has a different value for a leaf, or adds a new leaf, the patch has a leaf at that path with the new value. When a leaf exists in the original but not in the update, the patch has a leaf with the JSON value null, which deletes that element from the original. The patch has no entry for any leaf with the same value in both versions. If all leaf values are simple scalars, this is a compact representation of a change. It is less efficient when leaf values are arrays, because a merge patch replaces an array in its entirety even if only one entry changed.

JSON patch (RFC 6902) addresses the two weaknesses of merge patch. It defines a set of operators to modify a JSON object, so it can insert or delete one element of an array rather than resending the array. It can also change a value to null, which merge patch cannot do, because merge patch reads a null as an instruction to remove the element. That matters because some ALTO resources can have null values. JSON patch is less compact than merge patch for cost map updates, since each change becomes a separate operation with its own path.
sections.plainLanguage: A merge patch is the smaller of the two encodings: it lists the values that changed and uses null to mean delete. A JSON patch is a list of edit operations, each naming the exact place to change. Merge patch is easier for cost maps, and JSON patch is better when you need to touch one item inside an array or set a value to null.

sections.title: The Three Parts of the Design
sections.content:
The design has three parts. The update stream service is the building block: a POST-mode service that provides update streams. The client establishes a persistent connection and submits an initial update-stream request, which creates the stream. A stream can carry updates for GET-mode resources such as network and cost maps and for POST-mode resources such as the endpoint property service. To avoid creating too many streams, a client may use one stream for several requests, and it may even request updates for the same resource with different parameters for a POST-mode resource. The client therefore assigns a unique substream-id when it requests updates to a resource, and the server puts that substream-id in each update it sends for that resource. Each part of a stream is called a substream.

The stream control service handles changes that the client starts rather than the server. The client uses it to ask the update stream server to send updates for more resources, to stop sending updates for some resources, or to close the stream gracefully. The stream control server creates a new stream control resource for each update stream instance, assigns it a unique URI, and sends that URI to the client as the first event in the stream.

The Information Resource Directory (IRD) is where the services are announced. The IRD of an ALTO server defines the update stream services and declares the set of resources for which each one provides updates, and the server selects that set. It is recommended that if a resource depends on other resources, indicated by the uses attribute, those other resources are part of the same update stream. An update stream for a cost map should therefore also provide updates for the network map that cost map depends on. Because each stream consumes resources on the server, the server may require client authorization or authentication, limit the number of open streams, close inactive streams, or redirect a client to another update stream server.
sections.plainLanguage: The server offers update streams, the client asks for one with a POST request, and the connection stays open. Inside one stream the client can follow several resources at once by giving each one a substream number. A second service, whose address the server hands over in the first event, lets the client change the subscription while the stream is running.

sections.title: Data Update and Control Update Messages
sections.content:
Both kinds of update message sent from the server to the client share the same basic structure. Each carries a data field with the information, usually a JSON object, and an event field before it that says how the data is encoded. The event field of an ALTO update message can have two subfields, separated by a comma: media-type [ ',' data-id ]. The comma is not allowed in a media type name, so there is no ambiguity when decoding the two subfields. An update message does not use the SSE id field.

A data update message is sent when a monitored resource changes. Its media-type subfield says whether the data is a full replacement or an incremental patch. A full replacement uses the encoding defined by the resource's own document, such as the network map and cost map messages of RFC 7285, with that document's media type. The two incremental encodings are application/merge-patch+json and application/json-patch+json. The data-id subfield identifies the ALTO data the message applies to. When the resource holds a single JSON object, the data-id is the substream-id. When the resource is a multipart response, the data-id is the substream-id, a full stop, and the Content-ID of the part.

A control update message notifies the client of control information about the stream, for example that the server has stopped sending updates for a resource because it is overloaded or because the client asked for that. It has the media type application/alto-updatestreamcontrol+json and its data is an object with the optional members control-uri, started, stopped and description. The control-uri is the URI providing stream control for this stream. The message that carries it is sent once and MUST be the first event in an update stream. If the value is null, the update stream server does not support stream control for that stream. The started and stopped lists give the substream-ids of resources the server will start or stop sending updates for, and description is a human-readable explanation, which the RFC recommends the server use when it stops sending updates for a resource.
sections.plainLanguage: Every update is one Server-Sent Event with two parts. The event name says how the data is encoded and which subscription it belongs to. The data part holds the new map, or the patch that turns the old one into the new one. A separate kind of event carries control information, such as the address of the control service.

sections.title: The Update Stream Service
sections.content:
An update stream service is requested with the HTTP POST method and returns the media type text/event-stream. The client sends a POST body with the media type application/alto-updatestreamparams+json, containing a JSON object whose add member maps substream-ids to the resources the client wants updates for. Each entry can name the resource-id, an optional tag giving the version of the resource the client already holds, an optional incremental-changes flag, and an input object for a POST-mode resource that needs parameters.

The incremental-changes flag defaults to true. When it is true, the client MUST support all the incremental methods the server announced for that resource in its capabilities. A client that supports only some of them sets the flag to false, and the server then MUST NOT send incremental changes for that substream; it must send a full replacement instead. The client cannot suppress full replacement, because the server must always be able to send it.

If the request has errors, the server MUST NOT create an update stream and MUST return an HTTP 400 Bad Request with the generic ALTO error response format. A request with no add field, or with an add field that names no resource, produces the error code E_MISSING_FIELD with the field name add. A resource-id that is invalid or is not part of the update stream produces E_INVALID_FIELD_VALUE. In both cases the server closes the stream without sending any events.

The order of events is fixed. The first event MUST be the control update message carrying the control URI. If the client did not give a tag for a requested resource, the server MUST first send a full replacement for it; with a tag, the client can accept incremental changes and the server MAY omit the initial full replacement. If one resource depends on another, the update for the dependency MUST come first, so that when a network map changes the network map update precedes the cost map updates. If several clients open streams from the same update stream resource with the same request parameters, the server MUST send them the same updates, although it MAY pack the changes into a different number of events as long as the result is the same.

To keep the connection alive, an update stream server SHOULD send a comment line or an event every 15 seconds. A line starting with a colon is a comment and the client MUST ignore it. The RFC notes that the interval between TCP keep-alive messages depends on the operating system configuration and varies, so the recommended SSE keep-alive lets the client detect the state of the update stream server with more certainty.
sections.plainLanguage: The client posts a list of the resources it wants to follow, and the server starts the stream with a control message, then the current version of each resource. After that the server sends changes as they happen. The client can say it only wants whole new versions, which is simpler but uses more bandwidth, or it can accept patches, which are smaller but require more work at the client.

sections.title: The Stream Control Service
sections.content:
A stream control service lets the client remove resources from the set a stream is monitoring, add more resources, or shut the stream down. The client cannot discover the service through the IRD. Instead, the first event the update stream server sends carries the URI for the service associated with that stream. Each stream control request is an individual HTTP request, using the POST method, and the client MAY send several over the same HTTP connection.

The control service accepts the same input media type and parameters as the update stream service, and additionally accepts a remove field holding an array of substream-ids the client previously added. An empty remove array is treated as a request to remove all currently active resources, in which case the server closes the stream. The client MAY also use the add field to add resources, assigning a unique substream-id to each. Substream-ids MUST be unique over the lifetime of the stream, and the client MUST NOT reuse a substream-id that was removed before.

The server processes the add field before the remove field. If a request removes every active resource without adding any, the server MUST close the update stream, so a stream can never have zero resources. If the request has errors, the server MUST NOT add or remove any resources and MUST return an HTTP 400 Bad Request with the ALTO error response format. A substream-id in remove that was never added, or a substream-id in add that was used before in the same stream, produces the error code E_INVALID_FIELD_VALUE. If the associated update stream has been closed, the server returns an HTTP 404 Not Found. On success the server should return either an HTTP 202 Accepted or an HTTP 204 No Content response. The difference is that with 204 the server is sure the update stream server has also processed the request. Either way the final updates are notified by the update stream server through its own control update messages.

The URI of a control service MUST uniquely specify the update stream instance it controls, and the server MUST NOT use other properties of the request, such as cookies or the client's IP address, to determine the stream. A control URI must not be reused once its stream is closed.
sections.plainLanguage: The control service is a second, ordinary HTTP endpoint. The client posts to it to add or drop subscriptions, or to close the stream. The server answers with an accepted or no-content status, and the real effect shows up in the stream itself as a control event.

sections.title: Operational and Processing Considerations
sections.content:
The update schedule affects both overhead and freshness. To keep overhead down, the server may batch a sequence of updates for resources that change often, by sending cumulative updates or a full replacement after a while. Batching reduces freshness, so the server must weigh that against the delay it imposes on clients waiting for updates of dependent resources.

For cost maps, endpoint costs and endpoint properties, JSON merge patch is clearly superior to JSON patch: it is more space efficient and simpler to apply, and there is no advantage in allowing JSON patch for those resources. For network maps the choice is less clear. A small change, such as moving a prefix from one PID to another, is a simple insertion and deletion in JSON patch, while merge patch has to replace the whole array of prefixes for both PIDs. Against that, using JSON patch on network maps forces the client to keep the array indexes of the prefixes for each PID, even though the prefixes in a PID are logically an unordered set and the client has no other use for those indexes. A larger change, such as removing half the prefixes from a PID, is a new array under merge patch and a list of remove operations under JSON patch. Each server may therefore decide for itself which to use, based on the changes in network maps.

On the client side, a full replacement replaces the current version, and an incremental change is applied to it. Because resources can depend on others, the client MUST NOT use a dependent resource once the resource it depends on has changed. It can either buffer the change and apply all of them atomically, or update the network map immediately and mark each dependent cost map temporarily invalid until an update arrives that is based on the new network map version tag. If the expected updates never arrive, a simple recovery is to close the stream, discard the dependent resources, and re-establish the stream, optionally giving the version tags of the last versions held so that the server need not resend resources that are still current.
sections.plainLanguage: Batching changes keeps bandwidth down but makes the information less fresh. The client also has to be careful: when the network map changes, the cost maps that depend on it are out of date until their own updates arrive. The simplest way to be safe is to hold both back and apply them together.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations of the base ALTO protocol fully apply, including its authenticity and integrity considerations and the privacy considerations for ALTO users. The additional services, update streams and stream control URIs, extend the attack surface that the base protocol describes.

Persistent update stream connections enable a new class of denial-of-service attack. A client might create an unreasonable number of update stream connections, or add an unreasonable number of substream-ids to one stream. The server SHOULD limit the number of active streams and reject new requests when that threshold is reached. It SHOULD also limit the number of active substream-ids on a stream, or the total number used over the lifetime of a stream, and reject any stream control request that would exceed those limits. In these cases the server SHOULD return the HTTP status 503 Service Unavailable. The server may also prefer to restrict the update stream service to authorized clients, or return an HTTP 307 Temporary Redirect to another ALTO server that can handle the load.

Continuous updates can also overload the client, especially one with limited processing capability. The current design has no flow control mechanism for the client to reduce the update rate. Under overload the client may choose to remove the information resources that change most often, and it should be careful in how it uses information that may have become stale.

An outside party that can read the update stream response, or that can observe stream control requests, can obtain the control URI and use it to send fraudulent remove requests, disabling updates for the legitimate client. Encrypting the update stream and the stream control requests avoids this, and the server also echoes remove requests on the update stream so the legitimate client can detect unauthorized ones. Because the architecture allows the update stream server and the stream control server to be different entities, the private path between them should be protected with confidentiality, authenticity and integrity mechanisms.
sections.plainLanguage: Long-lived connections give attackers a new way to overload a server, so the server should cap how many streams and subscriptions it accepts and answer 503 when the cap is reached. The client also has no way to slow the server down, so a busy server can overwhelm a small client. The control URI is a secret of its own, and the stream should be encrypted so that nobody else can use it to stop the updates.
